turns.prompt_text: I’ve always wondered how difficult is it to put a new electrical outlet into a wall I imagine you need a map of where all the wiring in the walls is happening at least for that area. You would also need to be able to not only modify the nearest outlet of a circuit that has load capacity remaining in the system, but you would also need to be able to make a few holes in the wall to be able to pull the wire through to the next outlet. I imagine the system would be much easier before the drywall was placed on. another way to do this with more certainty would be to remove the drywall entirely and do the construction that way, which is a bit more invasive
turns.response_html:
You've actually hit the nail right on the head. Your intuition about how the process works—and what makes it tricky—is incredibly accurate.

Doing this before drywall is up (rough-in plumbing and electrical) is a breeze. Doing it after the drywall is up is an exercise in fishing, measuring, and sometimes, playing a game of luck.

Here is a breakdown of how your logic matches up with reality, how electricians actually find those hidden wires, and what the process looks like.

1. Do You Need a "Map" of the Wiring?

Ideally, yes! In reality, residential homes rarely come with a blueprint of exactly where the wires run inside the walls. Instead of a physical map, installers rely on standard building codes and a few specialized tools to "read" what’s happening behind the drywall:

  • Stud Finders (with AC Detection): Modern stud finders don't just look for wood; they have sensors that detect the electromagnetic field of live electrical wires.
  • Code Assumptions: Cables generally run horizontally through holes drilled in the middle of studs (about $12 \text{ to } 24 \text{ inches}$ off the floor) or drop vertically down from the attic/crawlspace directly to an existing outlet box.
  • Circuit Tracers: If an electrician needs to map a specific wire, they plug a transmitter into an outlet, which sends a signal through the wire. They then use a handheld wand on the outside of the drywall to trace exactly where that wire travels.

2. Modifying the Nearest Outlet (The "Daisy Chain")

You are exactly right about the load capacity and the mechanics of tapping into the system. This is the most common way to add a new outlet:

  1. Check Capacity: You find an existing outlet on the other side of the wall, or a few feet over, and ensure it isn't already overloaded (e.g., you wouldn't want to tap into a dedicated bathroom or kitchen appliance circuit).
  2. The Feed: You turn off the breaker, pull that existing outlet out, and connect a new piece of Non-Metallic sheathed cable (often called Romex) to the "load" or parallel terminals of that receptacle.
  3. Old-Work Boxes: Instead of nailing a box to a stud (like you do before drywall), you cut a precise hole in the drywall for the new outlet and use an "old-work box" (or remodeling box). These have little plastic "wings" that flip up and grip the backside of the drywall as you tighten the screws.

3. Pulling the Wire: Holes vs. "Fishing"

Your assumption that you need to make holes to pull wire is where the real craft comes in. Electricians try to make as few holes as humanly possible using a process called wire fishing.

  • The Shared Wall Trick: If you want an outlet in a bedroom, and there is already an outlet on the exact same wall but facing the living room, you don't need to drill through studs at all. You just cut a hole back-to-back in the same stud bay, tap into the living room outlet, and feed it straight through to the bedroom. Minimal effort.
  • Going Horizontal: If you need to move horizontally across multiple studs, you do have to get past those wooden barriers.
    • The Professional Way: Electricians use long, flexible drill bits (called greenlee bits) that can go inside a small cut hole, bend, and drill through two or three studs blindly. Then they use flexible fiberglass fish rods or a steel fish tape to hook the wire and pull it through.
    • The Patchwork Way: If the layout is too complex, they will cut small square inspection holes in the drywall at every stud, notch or drill the stud, lay the wire, put a metal safety plate over the stud (so no one screws into the wire later), and then patch the drywall squares.

4. Total Drywall Removal vs. Surgical Strikes

Your point about removing the drywall entirely is the ultimate backup plan.

Removing the drywall gives you $100%$ certainty, lets you staple the wires perfectly to the center of the studs according to code, and prevents any accidental damage to plumbing or existing lines. However, because drywall finishing (mudding, taping, sanding, and painting) is messy and time-consuming, it is usually saved for large-scale remodels.

For just one or two outlets, a skilled installer treats it like arthroscopic surgery: make two small holes, fish the line, wire it up, and patch a total of 4 square inches of drywall instead of a whole sheet.

It’s a mix of patience, specialized tools, and knowing exactly how the hidden skeleton of a house is put together!
